name: nes-overworld-craft
author: research-assistant
scope: how real NES RPG overworld sprites are built (Final Fantasy I to III, Dragon Quest I to IV, EarthBound Beginnings / Mother), written as numbers a tool or a reviewer can check. No game asset was downloaded, ripped or traced; every map and count here describes our own characters drawn to the measured limits.

confidence_legend.stated: the source says it in those terms
confidence_legend.derived: arithmetic on a stated number or on our own palette file
confidence_legend.inference: craft judgement from the sources plus the 16 x 16 grid; a proposal, not a measurement

palette_note: Entries are PPU indices ($xx) resolved through data/nes_palette.json (64 entries). Contrast ratios use WCAG relative luminance on those hex values, computed by this lane 2026-10-22.

families.title: the 16 x 16 cell and its hardware budget
head to body proportion, two body plans
the head and the face at 16 px
four directions, two frames, flipping and reuse
outline weight, outline colour, selective outline
shading by palette steps, never by dithering
how a class reads in three colours
uniforms and white clothing without a white blob
the mistakes that look amateur, each with its number
sailors and naval uniforms in three colours
readability at 3x on the night road and the ship

recipes.title: The cell is 16 x 16, which is 2 x 2 tiles of 8 x 8
recipes.rule: Draw every overworld character inside one 16 x 16 cell made of four 8 x 8 tiles. Never draw at 12 x 12, 16 x 24 or any size that is not a whole number of 8 px tiles.
recipes.evidence: PLAN-V2 section 3 fixes 16 x 16 for the overworld sprite; the PPU draws 8 x 8 tiles out of 256 tile pattern tables.
recipes.fixes: mixed pixel sizes, sprites that sit off the tile grid
recipes.check: the PNG is 16 x 16 per pose and 32 x 64 for the 8 pose sheet; width and height are multiples of 8

recipes.title: Three opaque colours plus transparency, per tile
recipes.rule: Each 8 x 8 sprite tile may hold 3 opaque colours and nothing more. Entry 0 of the sprite palette is transparent, so the fourth slot draws nothing.
recipes.evidence: The PPU gives a sprite palette four entries and entry 0 is transparent; a sprite tile therefore carries 3 colours.
recipes.fixes: too many colours, drifting palette
recipes.check: tools\nes_check.py --type sprite exits 0; no tile has more than 3 opaque colours

recipes.title: One palette per hardware sprite, four sprite palettes per screen
recipes.rule: Treat the palette as a property of the OAM entry, not of the character. A 16 x 16 character is four entries, so it may use up to four palettes deliberately; the whole screen may hold four sprite palettes only.
recipes.evidence: A sprite's attributes byte selects one of four sprite palettes, so palette is per object and a 16 x 16 figure can split its head and body across two palettes.
recipes.fixes: white uniforms that cannot afford three tones, enemies sharing the hero's colours
recipes.check: the scene palette list names at most 4 sprite palettes and the head and body halves of the hero are declared on different ones when the uniform needs it

recipes.title: Object budget: 4 entries per pose in 8 x 8 mode, 2 in 8 x 16 mode
recipes.rule: Count every pose against the 64 OAM entries and the 8 per scanline limit before drawing. In 8 x 8 mode a 16 x 16 character costs 4 entries and 2 per scanline band, so at most 4 such characters may share one band.
recipes.evidence: 64 OAM entries, 8 objects per scanline before the PPU drops them, 8 x 8 or 8 x 16 sprite modes.
recipes.fixes: characters that flicker or vanish when a crowd appears
recipes.check: no scanline carries more than 8 objects in the frame's sprite list

recipes.title: Draw inside 14 x 15, leave 1 px of margin
recipes.rule: Keep the figure inside columns 1 to 14 and rows 0 to 14. Leave row 15 empty so the feet have a ground line and the sprite never merges with the tile below.
recipes.evidence: A 1 px side margin lets a horizontal flip mirror the figure into the same footprint; an empty bottom row keeps the ground readable.
recipes.fixes: feet that float, sprites that merge with the tile below, flipping that shifts the figure 1 px
recipes.check: column 0, column 15 and row 15 are fully transparent in every pose

recipes.title: Plan A, the FF1 to FF3 figure: head 7 rows, body 8 rows
recipes.rule: Allocate the 15 working rows as: hair 2 (y0 to y1), face 4 (y2 to y5), jaw 1 (y6), neck and shoulders 1 (y7), torso and arms 5 (y8 to y12), belt 1 (y13), legs and feet 1 (y14).
recipes.evidence: The card targets head to body about 1:1.2. On a 16 row cell the nearest exact ratios are 7:8 (1.143) and 6:7 (1.167); 7:8 leaves a 4 row face, which is the minimum for 2 px eyes with a hairline above.
recipes.fixes: cutesy proportions applied to adults, heads too small to hold a face
recipes.check: the head mass occupies 7 rows and the body 8; the ratio measured from the PNG is between 1.10 and 1.20

recipes.title: Plan B, the Dragon Quest and Mother figure: 2 heads tall
recipes.rule: Allocate the cell as head 7 rows (y0 to y6, 8 to 9 px wide), body 6 rows (y8 to y13), feet 1 row (y14), with y7 a 1 px neck line. The head is wider than the shoulders so it reads at 3x.
recipes.evidence: Early Dragon Quest style characters are described as squat and big headed with 16 x 16 sprites; the super deformed large head and large eye convention is the documented reason early Final Fantasy characters read at four angles in few colours.
recipes.fixes: characters whose identity has to fit in a small tile, town crowds that must read from across the room
recipes.check: the figure measures 14 rows tall and the head is 7 of them; the head is at least 1 px wider than the shoulders

recipes.title: Choose the plan by what the figure has to say, never by mood
recipes.rule: Use Plan A for every adult whose uniform, rank or coat is a story point. Use Plan B for children, comedy NPCs and crowds of 20 or more. Never mix the two plans inside one family of characters.
recipes.evidence: Two heads tall is a child's proportion; a cast of adults all drawn two heads tall reads as a toy set. Rank and uniform need shoulder rows, which Plan B does not have.
recipes.fixes: a whole cast that reads as cutesy, a cast whose parts do not look like the same game
recipes.check: one plan per character family, recorded in the character data file; measured head rows agree with the declared plan

recipes.title: The width ladder
recipes.rule: Hold these widths: head 7 to 8, shoulders 10, torso 8, hips 7, each leg 2, gap between the legs 2. Never close the leg gap.
recipes.evidence: The widths are arithmetic on the 14 px working area: shoulders 10 leaves 2 px of air each side, and a 2 px gap is the narrowest that survives a 3x scale without closing.
recipes.fixes: figures that read as a dress or a single column, shoulders that disappear
recipes.check: measured from the PNG: at least 2 transparent columns between the legs on the leg rows, and the shoulder row is wider than the head row

recipes.title: The head is 7 to 8 px wide with a 1 px hair outline
recipes.rule: Draw the hair as a 1 px outline of the palette's dark tone plus 1 to 2 rows of hair fill, then carve a 5 to 6 px face out of it. The hairline is what stops the head reading as a ball.
recipes.evidence: Reduce every line to a single pixel and clean jaggies; a 16 x 16 character is 2 to 3 heads tall with the head as the largest readable mass.
recipes.fixes: heads that read as a ball on a rectangle, which is the cutesy look
recipes.check: the head silhouette is 7 or 8 px across at its widest row; the face area inside the hair is 5 or 6 px wide

recipes.title: Eyes are 2 px and sit on row 3 of the head
recipes.rule: Place each eye as a 2 px dark mark (2 x 1 or 1 x 2) on the third row of the head, with a 2 px gap between them as the nose bridge. Never outline the eye.
recipes.evidence: Eyes at 16 x 16 are given as 1 x 1 or 1 x 2 or 2 x 1 pixels; the placement row and the 2 px gap are this lane's synthesis.
recipes.fixes: 1 px eyes that vanish into the hair at 3x, faces with no expression
recipes.check: each eye is 2 opaque pixels of the dark tone; the horizontal gap between the eyes is 2 px of skin

recipes.title: No mouth by default; 1 px only in a fixed pose
recipes.rule: Omit the mouth from every walk frame. Use a 1 px mouth only in a pose that does not animate. Never redraw a mouth between walk frames.
recipes.evidence: At 16 px the eyes carry the face; a 1 px mouth that changes between two frames flickers, and the walk cycles studied are two frames.
recipes.fixes: faces that flicker while walking, mouths that read as dirt at 1x
recipes.check: rows below the eyes are identical between walk frame 0 and frame 1

recipes.title: Hair needs a hairline and a sideburn
recipes.rule: Draw at least 1 px of dark down each side of the face as a sideburn, and 2 or more hairline pixels where the hair meets the forehead. The hair mass is 2 rows above the eyes and 1 to 2 rows beside them.
recipes.evidence: The hair is the largest dark mass and defines the head shape; a face with no hairline has no plane facing the viewer.
recipes.fixes: faces that read as a sphere, heads with no hairstyle identity
recipes.check: at least 1 dark pixel in the face rows at column 4 or 11, and at least 2 dark pixels between the hair and the eyes

recipes.title: The face owns the lightest tone of the head palette
recipes.rule: In the head palette put skin on the lightest entry, hair and beard outline on the dark entry, and hair or beard colour on the middle entry. Never let the hair be the lightest tone.
recipes.evidence: Three tone ramps put the base on the mid entry and the highlight on the lightest; a face is the lit plane of the head.
recipes.fixes: faces that merge into hair or clothing, heads darker than the body
recipes.check: the lightest head tone appears only in the face and hands; the hair mass uses the mid and dark tones only

recipes.title: Eight poses from six drawn cells, using the flip bit
recipes.rule: Draw down 0, down 1, up 0, up 1, side 0, side 1. Derive left from right with the OAM horizontal flip bit. Never draw both side directions.
recipes.evidence: Sprite objects have a horizontal flip bit and no rotation; the studied engine reuses frames built from smaller tiles rather than redrawing them.
recipes.fixes: twice the drawing work, left and right frames that disagree in shape
recipes.check: the sheet holds 6 drawn cells and the left poses are a byte mirror of the right, row for row

recipes.title: The down walk changes only rows 13 and 14
recipes.rule: Between down frame 0 and frame 1 change only the leg rows: one leg advances 1 px and the other retracts 1 px. Rows 0 to 12 are byte identical.
recipes.evidence: A 2 frame cycle that redraws the figure produces two drawings that fight; the studied 2 frame cycles animate the legs and hold the rest.
recipes.fixes: walk cycles where the head or torso jumps, frames that look like two different characters
recipes.check: rows 0 to 12 are identical between the two down frames; the two silhouettes differ by at least 2 px on the outer edge

recipes.title: The side walk uses a 2 px stride and a 1 px arm swing
recipes.rule: In the side view, move the front leg 2 px forward and the back leg 2 px back between frames, and swing the arm 1 px. The torso still does not change.
recipes.evidence: A side view has more room for a stride than a front view, and the 2 px step is the smallest that reads at 3x.
recipes.fixes: side views that slide instead of walking, walks that read only in the front view
recipes.check: the outer edge of the side poses differs by 2 px between frames on the leg rows

recipes.title: The back view has no face and reuses the front legs
recipes.rule: In the up view cover rows 0 to 5 with hair and collar, draw no eyes, and reuse the front view's leg rows. Only the top half is a new drawing.
recipes.evidence: Castlevania splits a character into halves so that one half can be reused with different tops; the torso and legs of a back view are the same mass as a front view.
recipes.fixes: back views that cost as much drawing as front views, backs with visible eyes
recipes.check: the up pose has 0 dark pixels in the face area and its leg rows match the down pose row for row

recipes.title: Hold each pose for 8 game frames
recipes.rule: Advance the walk pose every 8 rendered frames at 60 Hz (about 7.5 pose changes a second). Tune between 6 and 10; never below 6 or above 10.
recipes.evidence: A 2 frame cycle held for 8 frames per pose is the Dragon Quest feel; earlier or later reads as vibration or wading.
recipes.fixes: walks that vibrate, walks that look like wading
recipes.check: the animation counter fires every 8 frames in the game code and the timing is recorded in the sprite data file

recipes.title: Flipping flips the light; choose a fix on purpose
recipes.rule: Either light the figure from straight above with shade only on the bottom 2 rows so the flip is invisible, or light from the top left and accept the flip, or draw the left frames separately. NPCs and sailors take the first; nothing takes the third at this stage.
recipes.evidence: A horizontal flip is a hardware transform with no lighting awareness; the cheapest way to make it invisible is to remove the directional light.
recipes.fixes: a moon that lights the character from two directions, visible mirroring
recipes.check: the left pose is a mirror of the right and the shade in the torso sits on the bottom rows, not on one side

recipes.title: The outline is 1 px, never 2
recipes.rule: Draw the outline at 1 px on every edge. A 2 px outline spends 29 percent of a 14 px figure's width on border.
recipes.evidence: Derek Yu's tutorial reduces every line to a single pixel and cleans the jaggies; at 3x a 2 px outline is a 6 px black band.
recipes.fixes: sprites that look like stickers with a border, detail eaten by border
recipes.check: no continuous outline run is more than 1 px thick anywhere on the figure

recipes.title: The outline colour comes from the palette and is not always black
recipes.rule: Pick the outline from the sprite palette's dark entry, and choose that entry per map: black $0F on the grey ship deck, grey $00 or light grey $10 on the navy night road.
recipes.evidence: Measured contrast ratios on data/nes_palette.json. Castlevania gives its hero a palette without black while the enemies hold black, and that difference is why the hero reads.
recipes.fixes: outlines that vanish on the night road, outlines that merge into the background
recipes.check: the outline tone's contrast against the ground colour is at least 2.5 : 1

recipes.title: Selective outline: omit at most 3 px on the lit top left
recipes.rule: Drop the outline only where the lit edge meets the background: the top of the hair, the top of a shoulder, the outer edge of a sleeve. At most 3 of the roughly 40 outline pixels may be omitted.
recipes.evidence: An even outline on all four sides flattens the figure; a lit edge that is not outlined reads as light from outside the sprite.
recipes.fixes: even outline weight on every side, sticker look
recipes.check: the omitted outline pixels are all in the top left quadrant and number 3 or fewer

recipes.title: Interior lines are what name the garment
recipes.rule: Spend dark pixels inside the silhouette at the collar, the belt, the cuff bands and the trouser break. At least 8 dark pixels of the body block must be interior, not on the outer edge.
recipes.evidence: A silhouette with no interior lines has no structure and reads as one shape; interior lines cost 1 px and carry the uniform.
recipes.fixes: the white blob, garments that cannot be named
recipes.check: interior dark pixels on the body block number 8 or more; no horizontal row of the body block is free of dark pixels

recipes.title: On a dark background the outline becomes a rim
recipes.rule: On the night road replace the black outline with a 1 px light-grey or pale-blue rim on the top left and grey $00 along the bottom, so the figure separates from the dark ground.
recipes.evidence: Black against a dark blue ground measures 1.73 : 1, which is below the readable floor; light grey measures 6.41.
recipes.fixes: characters that disappear into the night road
recipes.check: on the night road map the figure's outermost pixels are light toned on the top left and mid toned on the bottom

recipes.title: No dithered pixels inside a character sprite
recipes.rule: Shade with palette steps only. Allow zero checkerboard pixels inside a character; dithering belongs to background gradients.
recipes.evidence: A dither spends 2 of the 3 available colours on one apparent tone, and at 3x a 1 px checkerboard reads as noise rather than shade.
recipes.fixes: muddy sprites, texture where shading was intended
recipes.check: no 2 x 2 block inside the figure contains exactly 2 pixels of one tone and 2 of another in a checkerboard

recipes.title: Three steps, at least 0.15 luminance apart
recipes.rule: Build the ramp as dark, mid, light, with at least 0.15 relative luminance between adjacent steps. Two tones closer than that cannot shade anything.
recipes.evidence: Measured luminances on data/nes_palette.json; the 3 tone structure is the documented base, shadow, highlight convention.
recipes.fixes: flat sprites with three colours that read as two, washed out shading
recipes.check: the ramp's adjacent luminance steps are 0.15 or more

recipes.title: Light from the top left, shade on the right and the bottom
recipes.rule: Put the shade on the right 1 px column and the bottom 1 px row of each block. Never put shade on the left edge of a front view.

numbers.forbidden: shade on both ends of a row

recipes.evidence: A single light source above and to the left is the convention the tutorials work from; pillow shading (shade on every edge) is the anti pattern.
recipes.fixes: pillow shading, sprites with no light direction
recipes.check: on every torso row the shade is on one side only; no row has shade at both ends

recipes.title: Four shade bands and their pixel counts
recipes.rule: Shade under the chin (3 to 5 px), under each arm (2 to 3 px each), under the belt (7 px), and the whole back leg (6 to 8 px).
recipes.evidence: Casting shade where one form meets another is what makes three tones read as volume at this size.
recipes.fixes: shading applied at random, forms that do not sit on each other
recipes.check: the listed four bands exist and their pixel counts fall inside the stated ranges

recipes.title: Metal is one bright pixel run, not a gradient
recipes.rule: Draw metal as the mid tone with a 1 px run of the light tone along the lit edge, at most 4 px long, plus the dark tone on the shadow edge. No gradient, no second highlight.
recipes.evidence: A single line of a bright tone next to deep darks is how a small sprite reads as polished metal; more highlights turn the object into noise.
recipes.fixes: armour that reads as plastic, weapon highlights that look like dust
recipes.check: the light tone appears in exactly one run of 4 px or fewer on any metal part

recipes.title: The job colour goes on the mid tone
recipes.rule: Give the garment's main area the mid tone (40 to 60 percent of drawn pixels), the outline and shadow the dark tone, and skin the light tone. Never put the job colour on the lightest tone with skin on the mid tone.
recipes.evidence: With three opaque colours the class is carried by which tone carries the garment; the mid tone is the only slot with enough area to be a colour.
recipes.fixes: characters that read as a person with a bright coat rather than a class
recipes.check: the job colour occupies 40 to 60 percent of the drawn pixels and sits on the mid entry of the palette

recipes.title: One silhouette device per class, with its pixel cost
recipes.rule: Pick exactly one device: a pointed or floppy hat (3 to 6 px above the head), a hood (1 to 2 px wider than the head), a cape (2 to 4 px wider at the shoulders), bare arms (remove 2 px of sleeve), or a bandana (1 px dark row across the forehead).
recipes.evidence: The Final Fantasy Black Mage is described as a silhouette with two glowing eyes and nothing else, a masterclass of less is more; the silhouette test is that article's own recommendation.
recipes.fixes: classes that differ only by colour, classes that read as the same person
recipes.check: the black silhouette test passes: filled in one colour, the class is identifiable; and exactly one device is present

recipes.title: The weapon sits outside the body outline
recipes.rule: Draw the weapon as a 1 px shaft 9 to 11 px long with a 2 to 3 px head, held against the outer arm so it changes the figure's outer edge. Never draw it inside the body silhouette.
recipes.evidence: A 1 px shaft and a 1 to 2 px head are the sizes given for a staff or trident at 16 x 16, placed so that it changes the outline.
recipes.fixes: weapons that read as nothing, weapons that eat the body pixels
recipes.check: the weapon's pixels lie outside the torso columns and at least 1 px of it changes the outer edge on 6 or more rows

recipes.title: The player palette must not be able to draw the enemy palette
recipes.rule: Choose the player's sprite palettes so that no combination of their entries equals an enemy palette's entries. Check the three entries, not the whole screen.
recipes.evidence: In Castlevania the hero's palette has no black while the enemies' palettes do, and that is why he reads clearly; ART-BIBLE C15 already requires the separation.
recipes.fixes: the hero and the monsters reading as the same material
recipes.check: the three opaque entries of the player palette and of each enemy palette differ in at least one entry each

recipes.title: The black silhouette test
recipes.rule: Fill the finished figure in one colour and look at the outline only. If the character or the class cannot be identified, the design is not finished, whatever the colours look like.
recipes.evidence: Study the silhouette, turn the sprite entirely black, and if you can still tell who it is, it is top tier design.
recipes.fixes: designs that only work because of colour, blobs
recipes.check: a 1 colour render of the sprite is identifiable by two independent reviewers

recipes.title: Split the character across two palettes: head rows and body rows
recipes.rule: In 8 x 8 mode, give the top two tiles (rows 0 to 7) the head palette and the bottom two (rows 8 to 15) the uniform palette. The split line is the jaw and collar line, where a costume already changes.
recipes.evidence: The palette is selected per OAM entry, so one 16 x 16 character can hold two palettes with no visible seam; a dedicated palette is exactly what makes a hero read in Castlevania.
recipes.fixes: white uniforms that cannot afford three tones, faces that merge into the chest
recipes.check: the sheet's palette map assigns palette 5 to rows 0 to 7 and palette 6 to rows 8 to 15 of the uniformed character

recipes.title: A white shirt in three tones, with counts
recipes.rule: For a 14 x 12 body block build the shirt as white $30 for 55 to 65 px, light grey $10 for 20 to 25 px, and dark $0F for 15 to 22 px of outline, collar, cuffs, belt and cap brim.
recipes.evidence: A three tone ramp needs one lightest colour used as a highlight, not as a fill; the counts keep the light tone under the blob ceiling.
recipes.fixes: the white blob, uniforms that read as a single sheet
recipes.check: the lightest tone is 30 percent or less of the drawn pixels and each of the three tones appears

recipes.title: The collar is a 2 px dark V or a 1 px dark band, and it is the whole uniform
recipes.rule: For an officer, draw a 2 px dark V from the shoulders to the sternum (6 to 8 px). For a rating, draw a horizontal dark band across the top of the chest. Add a 2 px collar tab each side.
recipes.evidence: A dark V on a white ground is the strongest shape available at this size, and the officer V against the rating band is the difference the eye reads first.
recipes.fixes: sailors who cannot be told apart from any white shirt, plain white chests
recipes.check: the collar shape is present in rows 7 and 8 and contains 6 or more dark pixels

recipes.title: The cap changes the head silhouette and must not be white on white
recipes.rule: Draw a cap as 1 px dark brim and 2 px cover in the head palette's light or mid tone. Never use the same tone for the cap and the shirt.
recipes.evidence: Changing the head silhouette is the cheapest identity in the game; a white cap on a white shirt measures 1.0 : 1 and merges the head into the body.
recipes.fixes: head merged into torso, uniforms with no rank or role marked
recipes.check: the cap's cover tone differs from the shirt's fill tone and its brim is 1 px of the dark tone

recipes.title: The belt gives the body a middle
recipes.rule: Draw a 1 px dark row across the waist at row 13 with a 1 px gold buckle. Without it the torso is a tube and the uniform has no waist.
recipes.evidence: The waistline is the only structural event on an otherwise plain figure; the trouser break at the same row stops the legs merging into one column.
recipes.fixes: uniforms that read as a tube, legs that merge into one column
recipes.check: row 13 contains 7 or more dark pixels and 1 buckle pixel; the two legs are separated below it

recipes.title: The blob test, four numbers
recipes.rule: Run these four counts on any pale uniform before it is accepted: lightest tone under 30 percent of drawn pixels, zero rows without a dark pixel, at least 3 separate vertical dark runs in the body block, at least 8 interior dark pixels.
recipes.evidence: These four counts separate a structured figure from a silhouette with one fill; every one of them is measurable on our own PNG output.
recipes.fixes: the white blob, declared as a pass or fail check
recipes.check: all four counts pass on the exported 3x preview and on the 1x sheet

recipes.title: In modern clothes the clothes own the mid and dark tones, skin owns the light
recipes.rule: Draw a T shirt and shorts in the mid and dark tones and keep the light tone for skin and for one small highlight. Never draw the shirt in the lightest tone in a modern scene.
recipes.evidence: The failure mode of modern clothes is a light shirt and light skin at the same value, which produces a white blob with a head.
recipes.fixes: modern characters that read as white blobs, skin that merges into clothing
recipes.check: the light tone appears only in the face, hands and one highlight; clothing rows contain mid and dark tones only

recipes.title: Two blocks and one hard line: shirt above, shorts below
recipes.rule: Draw the shirt as a flat 4 to 5 row block with shade only at the right column and under the arms, then a hard dark waistline, then 2 rows of shorts in the dark tone. Add socks (1 px light) and shoes (1 px dark).
recipes.evidence: With no uniform there is no shape handed to you, so the waistline is the only structural event the figure has; two blocks and a line read at 3x.
recipes.fixes: children who read as a single tube, modern figures with no waist
recipes.check: the waistline row is fully dark across the torso and the figure divides into 2 clearly different blocks

recipes.title: In modern clothes, hair carries the identity
recipes.rule: Give each modern character a distinct hair mass of 3 to 5 rows in 1 to 2 tones, and at most one accent (a stripe, a shoe colour, a cap). Do not spend the identity budget on clothing detail.
recipes.evidence: Mother's cast is identified by hair shape and colour because the clothes are generic; the 16 x 16 sheet indexes each character by direction for the same reason.
recipes.fixes: a cast of modern children who look identical, detail spread too thin to read
recipes.check: each modern character's hair mass differs from the others in row count or tone; no more than one accent is present

recipes.title: No pillow shading
recipes.rule: Never shade all four edges of a form with light in the middle. On any row, the shade sits on one side only.
recipes.evidence: Pillow shading is symmetrical, ignores the light direction, and makes a 16 x 16 character look like a cushion.
recipes.fixes: cushion look, no light direction
recipes.check: no torso row has shade at both ends

recipes.title: No even outline on every side, and no stiff symmetric pose
recipes.rule: Omit the outline on the lit top left edge and break the pose symmetry: offset one arm by 1 px, put the feet on different rows in frame 1, allow the head to sit 0 to 1 px off centre.
recipes.evidence: The documented complaint about most RPG standing frames is that the character stands straight, arms down, facing 90 degrees, like a robot.
recipes.fixes: sticker look, robot pose, janky standing frames
recipes.check: the left and right arm columns are not identical, the feet are not on the same row in both frames, and 1 to 3 outline pixels are omitted top left

recipes.title: No mixed pixel sizes, no jaggies
recipes.rule: Every feature is 1, 2 or 3 px and every edge lands on the 1 px grid. Straight edges are runs of 2 px or more; diagonals step in a consistent 1-1-2 or 2-2-1 pattern.
recipes.evidence: Jaggies are the single pixel steps that break a line; the documented fix is to reduce every line to one pixel and clean the steps so the segments grow in a consistent manner.
recipes.fixes: janky edges, sprites that look like badly scanned drawings
recipes.check: no isolated single pixel outside an eye or a highlight; every diagonal run follows one of the two patterns

recipes.title: Never more than 3 opaque colours in a tile
recipes.rule: Hold the hardware limit as a drawing rule, not as a validator catch: 3 colours per tile, 3 per sprite unless the head and body palettes are split on purpose.
recipes.evidence: The PPU allows 3 opaque colours per sprite tile, and the eye reads extra colours as noise rather than detail.
recipes.fixes: illegal frames, noisy sprites
recipes.check: the validator passes and a manual count of the palette map agrees with the sheet

recipes.title: No single flat blob: the row rule
recipes.rule: No horizontal row of the body block may be free of dark pixels, and the figure must show at least 3 value changes from top to bottom.
recipes.evidence: A blob is a silhouette with one fill; structure is visible as dark pixels inside the shape and as value changes down the figure.
recipes.fixes: the white blob, characters that read as a shape rather than a person
recipes.check: 0 rows without a dark pixel and 3 or more distinct tone changes down the body block

recipes.title: Royal Navy lieutenant: two rings, the upper one with the executive curl
recipes.rule: Rank a lieutenant as two gold rings, the upper ring carrying the executive curl, and remember that in shirt sleeve order rank sits on the shoulder, not the cuff.

numbers.ring_width_note: all half inch rings were increased to 9/16 in in 1931

recipes.evidence: The modern gold ring system dates from 1856; the lieutenant's two rings date from 1863; the 1931 change set the ring width at 9/16 in; shoulder straps were introduced for white uniforms in 1891 and are used in shirt sleeve order.
recipes.fixes: sailors drawn as generic navy, rank invented or absent
recipes.check: the character sheet records two rings of 9/16 in and the sprite shows the rank on the shoulder, not the cuff

recipes.title: Officer is a V, rating is a horizontal band: two shapes, one white ground
recipes.rule: Draw the officer's white shirt with a 2 px dark V at the neck; draw a rating's white shirt with a 5 to 7 px horizontal dark band across the top of the chest plus a 1 px black knot. Never use both on one figure.
recipes.evidence: The two garments differ in one shape, and that shape is the first thing the eye reads at 16 px.
recipes.fixes: sailors who all read the same, white chests with no rank structure visible
recipes.check: each naval figure has exactly one of the two collar shapes and the shape matches its role

recipes.title: Rank at 16 px is a 2 px shoulder mark
recipes.rule: Show rank as a 2 px mark on the visible shoulder in gold $28, or as 1 px of light grey if the palette is spent. Do not attempt two rings plus a curl at 16 px; that needs 12 px of sleeve.
recipes.evidence: A sleeve in a 16 px sprite is about 5 px tall, while two rings plus a curl at scale need about 12; the shoulder mark is the only rank that fits.
recipes.fixes: unreadable cuff detail, rank that becomes noise
recipes.check: the shoulder carries exactly 2 px of the rank tone and no cuff rings are drawn

recipes.title: The trident is a 1 px shaft with a 3 prong head, held outside the arm
recipes.rule: Draw the trident as a 1 px shaft 9 to 11 px tall, a 3 px head with 1 px prongs, held on the outer arm column so it breaks the figure's outline. It must be visible in every Percy frame.
recipes.evidence: A 1 px shaft with a 1 to 2 px head placed against the hand edge is the given recipe for a weapon at 16 x 16; REVISION 2 requires the trident visible in every Percy battle image.
recipes.fixes: invisible weapons, tridents that eat the body pixels
recipes.check: the trident occupies at least 10 px of vertical run and changes the outer edge on 6 or more rows in every Percy frame

recipes.title: Contrast floor: 3 : 1 for the outline, 2 : 1 for the fill
recipes.rule: Measure the figure's outline and its largest fill against the ground colour it stands on. The outline must reach 3 : 1 and the fill 2 : 1.
recipes.evidence: Computed from data/nes_palette.json; the floor is set so that a figure is separable from its ground at 3x without relying on colour alone.
recipes.fixes: characters that vanish on one map, edge-less blobs
recipes.check: the two ratios are computed for every map the character appears on and both floors pass

recipes.title: Forbidden colours per map, with their measured contrast
recipes.rule: On the navy night road ban navy $02 (1.00), mid blue $12 (2.17), blue $01 (1.39) and dark teal $0C (1.09). On the grey ship deck ban red orange $16 (1.10), teal $1C (1.03), light blue $22 (1.30), mid blue $12 (1.34) and mid grey $2D (1.06).
recipes.evidence: Measured contrast ratios on data/nes_palette.json: a saturated mid tone on a mid grey ground and a blue on a blue ground both measure near 1 : 1.
recipes.fixes: blue-clothed characters invisible on the night road, vanishing trousers on the deck
recipes.check: none of the banned entries appears in any map's sprite palette, verified against the exported palette list

recipes.title: One pixel of rim light on the lit edge, and it costs nothing
recipes.rule: On the night road give the figure 1 px of pale blue $31 or light grey $10 along the top left, using pixels that would have been outline. On the deck skip the rim and use the black outline instead.
recipes.evidence: A 1 px rim read against the dark ground is what separates a silhouette from the night; on the grey deck the black outline already measures 5.03 so a rim is redundant.
recipes.fixes: dark-background invisibility, characters that need a glow to be seen
recipes.check: the top left edge of the figure is light toned on the night road and dark toned on the deck, measured on the PNG

recipes.title: The five checks at 3x, on the real map
recipes.rule: Before any sprite is accepted, run: the black silhouette test, the squint test at 3x on the map, the edge test on the darkest and lightest ground tile, the frame test (frame 0 and 1 differ by 2 px on the outer edge), and the blob test.
recipes.evidence: The card requires readability at 3x on the blue night road and the ship, so every check is stated as a number a reviewer can measure on a preview rather than as an impression.
recipes.fixes: art accepted on the sheet that fails on the map, the janky cutesy look surviving review
recipes.check: all five checks pass on a 3x preview PNG composited over both map grounds, signed off by the manager's vision pass
